words.meaning: The doorstep of a home, where floor art is drawn: the line between the street outside and the family inside.
A drawing on the floor at the doorstep, made with rice flour, often around a grid of dots.
Dot. The grid of dots a kolam is drawn around.
Tangle. A sikku kolam is one line that weaves round every dot and joins up with itself.
The Tamil month from mid-December to mid-January, when kolams are at their biggest and best.
Floor drawing in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana. Plural: muggulu. Chukkala muggu is the dot kind.
A small mound of cow dung topped with flowers, set in the middle of a muggu at Sankranti.
Bengal's floor art, drawn in white rice paste with a fingertip or a bit of cloth.
Floor and wall drawings of Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh: white chalk lines on red earth.
Rice-paste floor drawings of Mithila, in Bihar, made for pujas and weddings.
Odisha's white rice-paste drawings on floors and walls, also called chita.
The goddess of wealth and good fortune, welcomed into homes at Diwali with lamps and rangoli.
Patterns on the floor in coloured powder, rice or petals. Often said to come from rang (colour) and aavali (row).
A carpet of flower petals laid at the door for Onam. Poo is flower; kalam is a drawing on the floor.
Kerala’s harvest festival in the month of Chingam (August–September), when King Mahabali is said to visit his people.
The first of the ten days of Onam, when the first small ring of flowers is laid.
The tenth and biggest day of Onam: the largest pookalam, new clothes and the Onam feast.
A tiny white flower that grows wild in Kerala. It is said to be Mahabali’s favourite, so many homes use it in the pookalam.
The generous king of the Onam story, said to come back once a year to see his people happy.
A feast of many dishes served on a banana leaf. The Onam one is the Onasadya.
Tie-and-dye: tiny knots are tied in the cloth before it is dyed, and each knot leaves a dot. From bandh, to tie.
A single dot: the simplest bandhani knot. Clusters of three, four and more have names of their own.
A Gujarati wedding sari, traditionally red, with bandhani dots set in a grid of squares.
Rajasthan’s wave tie-dye: the cloth is rolled and tied on the slant, so the colour comes out in diagonal stripes. Lehar means wave.
A dyer: the person who colours the cloth.
A carved wooden printing block · printing.
Families of hand block printers in Rajasthan and Gujarat. The name is linked to chhapna, to print.
A mud paste pressed onto cloth to keep dye off. It cracks as it dries, and the dye seeps in as fine veins.
Spotted or printed cloth. The English word chintz comes from it.
Line. In block printing, the outline block that goes on first; the colour blocks are cut to sit inside it.
A master of a craft, who takes on learners.
A learner who works beside an ustad, often for years, until the hand is ready.
The evil eye: the idea that an envious look can bring bad luck.
A scary face or charm hung on trucks, shops and new houses to catch the evil eye before it does harm.
A lemon and green chillies on a thread, hung at doors and on vehicles to keep bad luck away.
A picture, a photograph.
Script: a way of writing. India has more than a dozen in everyday use.
An ancient script, used in Emperor Ashoka’s inscriptions in the 3rd century BCE. Most scripts of India grew out of it.
A letter, or a syllable as it is written.
A baby’s naming ceremony.
A kolam whose line loops around the dots instead of joining them. Kambi means wire.
Dots in straight rows and columns, like a grid. Ner means straight.
Dots in staggered rows, each row tucked into the gaps of the one before.
The new-moon night, the darkest of the month. Diwali’s main night is an amavasya.
A small clay lamp: a cotton wick in oil or ghee. Rows of them are what Deepavali is named for.
A sparkler. Phool is a flower and a jhadi a shower: a shower of flowers.
A pomegranate, and the flowerpot firework that fountains sparks like the fruit bursting with seeds.
A ground spinner: a coil that whirls round on the floor throwing sparks. The toy’s Chakri mode spins every stroke six ways.
A demon king of the old stories, defeated by Krishna and Satyabhama. Naraka Chaturdashi, the day before Diwali, marks his end.
“Day of release”: Sikhs remember Guru Hargobind’s release from Gwalior Fort, celebrated at Diwali time.
A “sky lantern”: a paper lantern, often star-shaped, hung outside homes at Diwali.
A string puppet. Kath is wood and putli a doll: a doll made of wood.
Families of puppeteers in Rajasthan, who also kept the family histories of their patrons.
The little reed whistle a puppeteer speaks through, giving the puppet its squeaky voice. Boli also means speech.
The holder of the strings: the one who works the puppets, and in old Indian drama the director who opens the play.
A barrel drum with two heads played by hand: one low and booming, one high and ringing. The toy’s Nacho button plays one.
Karnataka’s string puppet theatre. Gombe is a doll and aata is play.
Bengal’s rod puppets. Putul is a doll and nach is dance.
Andhra’s leather shadow puppets. Tholu is leather and bommalata is doll play.
A warm, respectful Rajasthani greeting, said with folded hands, much like namaste.
An Adivasi people of the Sahyadri hills in Maharashtra, and the white wall paintings they are famous for.
“First dwellers”: the name many of India’s tribal communities use for themselves.
Red ochre: red earth used as a colour. Warli walls dry to this deep red-brown.
A long horn made from a dried bottle gourd and bamboo. Warli dancers circle round its player.
A square. In a Warli wedding painting, the square frame at the centre of the picture.
The Warli mother goddess of fertility, painted inside the dev chauk.
The sun’s journey north: Gujarat’s kite festival in mid-January, at Makar Sankranti.
The day the sun moves into Makara (Capricorn), around 14 January: a harvest festival across India.
A kite fight: two strings crossed, each flyer trying to cut the other.
Roughly “I have cut it!”: the shout when your kite cuts another kite’s string.
The little bridle of thread that ties a kite to its string. Where it is knotted decides how the kite flies.
The spool the kite string is wound on, held by a friend while you fly.
Kite string coated with paste and powdered glass, for cutting other kites. It also hurts birds and people.
Paper lanterns flown on kite strings on Uttarayan night.
